statement: In autistic adults with marked to very severe social anxiety (one randomized pilot trial at a single California site: 8 randomized to MDMA and 4 to an inactive placebo, of whom 7 and 4 were analysed), two MDMA sessions within psychotherapy, compared with placebo with the same psychotherapy, were followed one month later by a larger fall in interview-rated social anxiety (Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale: −44.1 vs −19.3 points; difference 24.8, 95% CI 1.9 to 47.9; P = 0.037), and the difference was similar at 6 months (P = 0.036). Participants identified their allocation in 22 of 23 sessions, two dose groups were pooled (in the registry the lower-dose group improved more), and the interval runs from a trivial to a very large difference, so the evidence is insufficient to say how much, if at all, MDMA reduces social anxiety in autistic adults. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small trial, 12 autistic adults with strong social anxiety had talking therapy with MDMA or a dummy pill. Social anxiety dropped more with MDMA, but almost everyone could tell which pill they had, and the trial was too small to show how big any benefit is.
population: Autistic adults aged 21 or older (ADOS-2 Module 4) with an LSAS of 60 or more, MDMA-naive by self-report, physically healthy and psychologically stable
exposure: MDMA in two blinded 8-hour sessions about a month apart (two dose subgroups, pooled), with three preparatory sessions including mindfulness skills and three integrative sessions after each
comparator: Inactive placebo (lactose) with the same psychotherapy
outcome: Change in Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale total from baseline to one month after the second session (primary) and to 6 months
magnitude: LSAS change −44.1 (SD 14.8; n = 7) vs −19.3 (18.8; n = 4); t(9) = 2.451, P = 0.037; 95% CI of the difference 1.92 to 47.87 (editors' recalculation 1.8 to 47.8); placebo-subtracted d 1.4, printed CI −0.074 to 2.874 (editors' approximation 0.04 to 2.76). Six months: −47.7 (14.7) vs −23.3 (18.0), P = 0.036. Fall of 20 points or more: 6 of 7 vs 2 of 4. Registry results by dose group: lower-dose group −51.0, higher-dose group −39.0, placebo −19.3.

evidence.extracted: LSAS: placebo 83.3 (11.9) at baseline and 64.0 (13.3) at the primary endpoint, change −19.3 (18.8); MDMA 91.8 (15.8) and 46.4 (15.2), change −44.1 (14.8); t(9) = 2.451, P = 0.037, CI 1.92 to 47.87; placebo-subtracted d 1.4 (CI −0.074 to 2.874); MDMA n = 7 after baseline.

evidence.locator: Results › Clinical response, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3
evidence.extracted: Six months: placebo change −23.3 (18.0), MDMA −47.7 (14.7); t(9) = 2.454, P = 0.036; within the MDMA group, primary endpoint to 6 months P = 0.307; a fall of 20 points or more in 6 of 7 on MDMA vs 2 of 4 on placebo (Table 3; the text gives 6 of 8).

Participants guessed their treatment wrongly in one of 8 placebo sessions and in none of the 15 MDMA sessions (correct in 22 of 23); the two therapists were wrong in 2 and 1 of 8 placebo sessions and in 2 of 15 MDMA sessions each.

evidence.locator: Fig. 1 (CONSORT diagram, image); Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Of 8 randomized to MDMA, one was withdrawn after randomization because they had been enrolled with hypertension and a recent substance use disorder within the exclusion window; 7 MDMA and 4 placebo participants were analysed, without imputation; the two dose subgroups were combined.

evidence.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02008396 (API v2) › Status; Results › Outcome Measures
evidence.extracted: Registered 6 December 2013, before the start on 11 April 2014; LSAS change to one month after session 2 posted by group: lower-dose MDMA group −51.0 (8.19), higher-dose group −39.0 (17.57), placebo −19.3 (18.77); posted denominators 4, 4 and 3, while weights of 3 and 4 reproduce the paper's pooled MDMA values (editors' calculation).

The authors call the sample small, too small to compare doses, consider blinding with an inactive placebo adequate because one participant and both investigators made incorrect guesses, and acknowledge that observable MDMA effects might contribute to efficacy.

risk_of_bias.note: Allocation evident in 22 of 23 sessions with a participant-reported interview outcome.

grade.reasoning: One randomized trial: starts high. Risk of bias two levels (very serious, RoB 2 high for the measurement of the outcome): the LSAS interview scores participants' own reports of fear and avoidance, and participants identified their allocation in 22 of 23 sessions, with no measure of expectancy; one MDMA participant was withdrawn after randomization. Imprecision two levels: 11 analysed, and the 95% interval of the difference runs from about 2 to 48 points (the printed interval for d reaches zero). Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to the trial population and endpoints. The relation is 'insufficient evidence' because the trial cannot show the size of any effect with precision; the statement reports the observed difference.
